courses.title: Internal Medicine I: Cardiology and Respiratory Medicine
courses.description: Hypertension, heart failure, rheumatic and ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmias, asthma, COPD, pneumonia, tuberculosis and pleural disease in Nigerian practice.

topics.title: Hypertension
topics.summary: Diagnosis, target-organ damage, treatment in Africans, and hypertensive emergencies.

material.heading: Diagnosis and evaluation
material.body: Hypertension affects about 30% of Nigerian adults and is the leading risk factor for stroke, heart failure and chronic kidney disease; most patients are unaware. Diagnosis: clinic BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg on repeated measurements (correct cuff size, seated, rested), ideally confirmed by ambulatory or home monitoring (excluding white-coat hypertension). Over 90% is primary (essential); secondary causes are suspected in young patients, resistant hypertension or suggestive features — renal disease, renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism (hypokalaemia), phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal symptoms), Cushing's syndrome, coarctation of the aorta, thyroid disease, and drugs (oral contraceptives, NSAIDs, steroids). Evaluation seeks target-organ damage: left ventricular hypertrophy (ECG, echo), retinopathy (fundoscopy — Keith–Wagener grades), proteinuria and renal function, and cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, lipids, smoking).
keyPoints: Target organs: heart, eyes, kidneys, brain

material.heading: Treatment
material.body: Lifestyle: salt reduction (< 5 g/day — high salt intake is common, including seasoning cubes), weight loss, regular exercise, limited alcohol, smoking cessation, diets rich in fruit and vegetables (DASH). Drug therapy in black Africans: calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) and thiazide(-like) diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide) are more effective first-line agents than ACE inhibitors or beta-blockers as monotherapy; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are added (and preferred in diabetes with proteinuria, CKD, heart failure). Single-pill combinations improve adherence. Target generally < 140/90 (< 130/80 in high-risk patients if tolerated). ACE inhibitors cause cough and angioedema (more common in black patients); avoid in pregnancy. Hypertensive emergency (severe BP with acute organ damage — encephalopathy, acute LV failure, dissection, eclampsia) requires controlled IV reduction (e.g. labetalol, hydralazine, nitroglycerin) by no more than about 25% in the first hour; hypertensive urgency without organ damage is treated with oral drugs.
keyPoints: CCB or thiazide first-line in Africans
ACEi angioedema more common in black patients

topics.title: Heart Failure and Cardiomyopathies
topics.summary: Causes in Africa, clinical features, classification, investigation and management.

material.heading: Causes and assessment
material.body: Heart failure (HF) is a syndrome of symptoms (breathlessness, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, ankle swelling) and signs (raised JVP, third heart sound, basal crackles, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly) due to cardiac dysfunction. In sub-Saharan Africa (THESUS-HF registry), leading causes are hypertensive heart disease, cardiomyopathies (dilated; peripartum cardiomyopathy — high incidence in northern Nigeria; endomyocardial fibrosis), rheumatic heart disease, and increasingly ischaemic heart disease; patients are younger than in high-income countries. Classification: HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, EF ≤ 40%), mildly reduced (41–49%) and preserved EF (HFpEF ≥ 50%). NYHA classes I–IV grade symptoms. Investigations: ECG, chest X-ray (cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, Kerley B lines, effusions), echocardiography (key test), natriuretic peptides (BNP/NT-proBNP), renal function, electrolytes, FBC and thyroid function.

material.heading: Management
material.body: Acute decompensated HF: sit upright, oxygen if hypoxic, IV furosemide, nitrates if BP adequate, treat precipitants (uncontrolled BP, infection, arrhythmia, non-adherence, anaemia, excess salt). Chronic HFrEF — prognostic 'four pillars': ACE inhibitor/ARB or ARNI (sacubitril–valsartan), evidence-based beta-blocker (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate — start low when stable), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone) and SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin); loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve survival; hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate benefits black patients (A-HeFT). Digoxin controls rate in atrial fibrillation. Devices (ICD, CRT) where available. Monitor potassium and renal function, daily weights, salt and fluid restriction, and vaccination. Peripartum cardiomyopathy may benefit from bromocriptine and requires contraception counselling.
keyPoints: Four pillars: ACEi/ARNI, BB, MRA, SGLT2i

topics.title: Rheumatic, Ischaemic and Other Heart Diseases
topics.summary: Rheumatic fever and valve disease, acute coronary syndromes, infective endocarditis and arrhythmias.

material.heading: Rheumatic and infective heart disease
material.body: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis in children (5–15 years), diagnosed with the revised Jones criteria — major: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules; minor: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval — plus evidence of recent streptococcal infection (ASO). Rheumatic heart disease most commonly affects the mitral valve (mitral regurgitation in the young, mitral stenosis later — loud S1, opening snap, mid-diastolic murmur; atrial fibrillation and stroke), then the aortic valve. Secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin prevents recurrence. Infective endocarditis: fever with a new murmur; Duke criteria (positive blood cultures — at least three sets before antibiotics — and echocardiographic vegetations); causes include Streptococcus viridans (dental), Staphylococcus aureus (IV drug users — tricuspid valve) and enterococci; prolonged IV antibiotics and sometimes surgery.

material.heading: Ischaemic heart disease and arrhythmias
material.body: Ischaemic heart disease is increasing in Nigeria with urbanisation, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and smoking. Acute coronary syndromes: STEMI (ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in two contiguous limb leads or ≥ 2 mm in chest leads, or new LBBB), NSTEMI (raised troponin without ST elevation) and unstable angina. Immediate management: aspirin 300 mg, a P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel), oxygen only if hypoxic, nitrates and opioid analgesia, anticoagulation, and reperfusion — primary PCI within 120 minutes (limited availability in Nigeria) or fibrinolysis (streptokinase, tenecteplase) within 12 hours of onset; then secondary prevention (aspirin, statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, lifestyle). Atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular pulse, absent P waves): rate control (beta-blockers, digoxin), rhythm control in selected cases, and stroke prevention with anticoagulation guided by CHA2DS2-VASc score. Complete heart block may need pacing.

topics.title: Asthma, COPD and Pneumonia
topics.summary: Obstructive airway diseases and community-acquired pneumonia.

material.heading: Asthma and COPD
material.body: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with variable, reversible airflow obstruction — episodic wheeze, cough (often nocturnal), chest tightness and breathlessness; triggers include dust, smoke, pollen, harmattan, infections, exercise and NSAIDs. Diagnosis: history plus evidence of variability (peak flow variability, bronchodilator reversibility ≥ 12% and 200 mL on spirometry). GINA recommends inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing treatment for all adults and adolescents — as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol or daily ICS with SABA reliever — stepping up to ICS–LABA and specialist therapies; SABA-only treatment increases risk of death. Acute severe asthma: inability to complete sentences, PEF 33–50%, RR ≥ 25, HR ≥ 110; life-threatening features — silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, PEF < 33%, SpO2 < 92%. Treat with oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, systemic steroids, IV magnesium, and ICU referral. COPD: persistent airflow limitation (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.7) from smoking or biomass smoke; management includes smoking cessation, bronchodilators (LAMA, LABA), pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and treating exacerbations with steroids and antibiotics when sputum is purulent.

material.heading: Pneumonia
material.body: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP): cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, focal crackles or bronchial breathing, and new consolidation on chest X-ray. Commonest cause is Streptococcus pneumoniae; others: Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza, cavitation), Klebsiella (alcoholics — upper lobe, 'red currant jelly' sputum), atypicals (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila), and viruses; consider TB and Pneumocystis in HIV. Severity: CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea > 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥ 30, BP systolic < 90 or diastolic ≤ 60, age ≥ 65) — 0–1 home, 2 hospital, ≥ 3 severe (consider ICU). Treatment: amoxicillin for low severity; amoxicillin or ceftriaxone plus a macrolide for moderate–severe; oxygen, fluids, analgesia. Complications: parapneumonic effusion, empyema (drain), lung abscess, sepsis. Aspiration pneumonia (right lower lobe) occurs with reduced consciousness or swallowing problems. Pneumococcal and influenza vaccines prevent disease.

topics.title: Tuberculosis and Pleural Disease
topics.summary: Pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB, TB–HIV, drug-resistant TB, pleural effusion and pneumothorax.

material.heading: Tuberculosis
material.body: Nigeria has one of the highest TB burdens globally and the highest in Africa, with many undiagnosed cases. Pulmonary TB: cough > 2 weeks, fever, night sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis; chest X-ray shows upper-lobe infiltrates and cavities (atypical in HIV). Diagnosis: Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra on sputum (first-line in Nigeria), smear microscopy (ZN), culture (gold standard; drug susceptibility testing), urine LAM in advanced HIV. Extrapulmonary TB: lymph nodes (commonest), pleura, spine (Pott's disease), abdomen, meninges and pericardium. Treatment: 2HRZE/4HR (6 months); longer for TB meningitis and spinal TB, with steroids in meningitis and pericarditis. Drug-resistant TB (rifampicin-resistant/MDR) uses all-oral short regimens (BPaLM). TB–HIV: test all TB patients for HIV; start ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment (delay 4–8 weeks in TB meningitis because of IRIS risk); give TB preventive therapy to eligible people living with HIV and household contacts.
keyPoints: Nigeria: highest TB burden in Africa

material.heading: Pleural disease
material.body: Pleural effusion: dullness to percussion ('stony dull'), reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance. Light's criteria distinguish exudates (pleural fluid protein/serum protein > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, or pleural LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH) from transudates. Transudates: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia. Exudates: TB (commonest in Nigeria — lymphocytic, high adenosine deaminase), parapneumonic effusion/empyema (pus, low pH < 7.2 and low glucose — drain), malignancy (breast, lung, lymphoma — often bloody). Diagnostic tap sends fluid for protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cells, Gram and ZN stains, culture and cytology; pleural biopsy may be needed. Pneumothorax: primary spontaneous (tall thin young men), secondary (COPD, TB, PCP), traumatic and tension (emergency — needle decompression then chest drain); small pneumothoraces may be observed, larger or symptomatic ones aspirated or drained.
